###### **Introduction** 

• **_Increasing concerns about the state of the global economy and rising levels of risk aversion are now leading us to expect higher gold prices, and for longer, than we had

hitherto been looking for. We believe gold could pierce $2,000 by year-end, and hold at elevated levels for at least the first half of 2012 as inflation fears tighten their grip on investor perceptions._** • **_Gold’s rally through $1,900 intra-day in late August was accompanied by some investment buying at a “grass roots” level as investors feared that the market was running away from them. The subsequent correction deterred buyers, but bullish sentiment prevails and we believe it is only a matter of time before fresh buying develops._** • **_Silver continued, in the main, to underperform gold as investors remained bruised by the viciousness of the price fall in May. The market still has to contend with a surplus of supply over fabrication demand, but the metal has been showing some signs of fresh investor interest and if gold runs towards $2,000 then silver could well test $50._** • **_Platinum has outperformed palladium in recent weeks and, while this is partly because of palladium’s prior outperformance, platinum has also been supported by fears of supply disruption from South Africa. **I1** Economic Indicators - September 2011 There were a number of disappointing economic numbers released during August and both business and consumer confidence levels fell. The associated reduction in consumer spending has, arguably, further weakened the putative economic recovery in North America and Europe, and equity markets suffered accordingly during much of August. Dr. Bernanke’s statement at the Jackson Hole policy-makers’ conference late in the month met a mixed reception. The equity markets picked up on the expectation that the September meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) would herald a further programme of economic support, although the nature of that likely support is still a subject of speculation. Treasury markets also picked up, though, in the belief that any recovery will be anaemic. There are still some fears that the US economy is headed for a double-dip recession. The minutes of the August meeting of the FOMC revealed divided opinions among Committee members about how best to address the faltering in the US economy. In the event, the minutes implied a kind of “holding pattern”, with a vote to keep short-term interest rates at just above zero until at least the middle of 2013. The Committee members noted that, while the effects of temporary factors such as the Japanese earthquake and the “damping effect” of higher energy and other commodity prices appeared to be waning, the “underlying strength of the economic recovery remained uncertain”. Some members pointed also to “the financial market strains seen during the inter-meeting period, as contributing to a downgrade of the outlook for the economy”. The run was swift and sharp, fuelled in part by technical trading (i.e. stoploss orders and momentum trades). It was followed by an equally sharp fall, but underlying sentiment remained positive towards gold, with the result that gold’s net change over the course

of August was a gain of $200 or 12%, with an opening fix of $1,613.50 and a closing fix of $1813.50. The second half of July saw gold prices contained in a relatively narrow range, but with a mild upward bias, between $1,580 and $1,625 (on an intraday basis). Early August saw a swift jump towards $1,680 following a number of weak economic indictors that fuelled expectations of a further round of quantitative easing. The move gained traction in the second week of August as fears increased over the possibility of a downgrade of French sovereign debt, due to that country’s exposure to European debt in the more heavily stricken nations, and prices jumped towards $1,815. After a brief correction gold then took off, gaining more than $120 in three days and clearing $1,900 on 23rd August. This move was, as noted above, extended by technical trading, but with sentiment also powered by disappointment at the outcome of the Franco-German summit with respect to how to tackle the problems in Europe. In percentage terms, however, the August 2011 fall was smaller than the January 1980 drop, at 6% of the previous day’s fix, compared with 13% in the earlier fall. On a year-on-year basis, the end-August fix represented a gain of $567.50 or 46% and as such, it could be argued that there is not much scope for further price gain. However, we take the view that the economic and financial environment remains strongly supportive of higher gold pr

ices, and that these higher prices are now likely to be sustained for longer than we had originally expected. For example: - The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) remains divided over the best course of action for underpinning the United States economy and a third round of quantitative easing cannot be ruled out, especially as the Federal Reserve Chairman Bernanke has now announced that the September FOMC meeting will be extended to two days, rather than the originally scheduled oneday programme. The minutes from the August FOMC meeting were released at the end of the month and showed that, after consideration of a range of options, the Committee had decided upon sustaining loose monetary policy at least through to mid-2013. This, allied to already bloated fiscal balance sheets, points to increasing inflationary pressures and by association a long period of negative real interest rates; both of these traditionally favour gold investment.
